source.title: DISTRIBUTED-APPLIANCE-FAB-001: qualify household and neighbourhood fabrication of repair parts
source.body:
Parent / composition:
- Symtropy [APPLIANCE-MICROFACTORY-001 #6603](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symtropy/issues/6603): first appliance manufacturing process, FDM fixtures, product cell and make/buy/partner decisions.
- Symtropy [APPLIANCE-QUAL-001 #1805](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symtropy/issues/1805): repairability, service life and independent replication.
- Symthaea [MFG-PROC-000 #5686](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symthaea/issues/5686): manufacturing process/capability/recipe/qualification semantics, including FDM and other AM methods.
- Symtropy [MFG-ARCH-PORTABILITY-001 #6579](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symtropy/issues/6579): portability of manufacturing information architectures.
- Symtropy [REPAIRABILITY-COMPILER-001 #1773](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symtropy/issues/1773): task-graph-based repair burden and restoration time.
- Symthaea [HABITAT-VERTICAL-001 #8051](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symthaea/issues/8051): factory-to-product-to-repair integration for household goods.
- Mycelix existing manufacturing, product identity, parts, repair and evidence owners remain authoritative for operational records and provenance.

## Objective

Design and validate a **distributed household-to-neighbourhood digital-fabrication network** that enables residents and local workshops to produce selected, rights-cleared, low-risk appliance replacement parts, accessories, jigs and fixtures on demand, while routing safety-critical and high-performance parts to qualified professional manufacturers.

This is not a programme to print entire household appliances in every home, not a claim that consumer FDM machines replace industrial manufacturing, and not permission for residents to reproduce electrical, pressure, thermal, structural or other safety-critical parts without qualified process and product evidence.

The core proposition is:

> Every repairable product should have an explicit, rights-cleared map of which parts may be locally fabricated, by which process/material/capability class, with what inspection, and what post-repair verification.

The network should include a household node where appropriate, neighbourhood fabrication hubs, and regional/industrial partners. Households should be able to participate without owning a printer.

## Why this is timely

### New standards directly relevant to distributed fabrication

- **ISO/ASTM 52966:2026**, published 2 November 2026, defines a level framework for additive-manufacturing capability in temporary self-sufficient systems, covering people, training, infrastructure, materials and the full part lifecycle. It explicitly considers on-site and onshore support. This is a useful reference for designing household / community / regional capability tiers, not a household product-safety standard:
  https://www.iso.org/standard/89300.html
- **ISO/ASTM 52951:2026**, published June 2026, defines data packages for AM parts from design through fabrication and acceptance. Its detailed requirements are based on metal laser powder-bed fusion, but its data-package / digital-thread concepts are relevant to our application-specific FDM profile:
  https://www.iso.org/standard/76828.html
- **ISO/ASTM 52900:2021** is the current AM fundamentals vocabulary standard and was confirmed in 2025:
  https://www.iso.org/standard/74514.html
- **ISO/ASTM 52902:2023** provides geometric capability test artefacts for AM systems:
  https://www.iso.org/standard/82056.html
- **ISO/ASTM 52924:2023** covers qualification/classification of polymer AM part properties:
  https://www.iso.org/standard/82959.html
- **ISO 27548:2024** defines a chamber test method for particle (including ultrafine-particle) and specified chemical emissions from desktop material-extrusion printers. The standard warns that its chamber test does not necessarily predict every real-world exposure and does not cover all possible feedstock emissions:
  https://www.iso.org/standard/83712.html
- **ISO/ASTM 52920:2023** concerns industrial AM processes and production sites; use it as an industrial-hub reference, not as a claim that a household printer is a qualified industrial production site.

### Health and safety boundary for domestic printers

NIOSH warns that desktop material-extrusion printers can emit ultrafine particles and volatile compounds. Its guidance prioritizes source control, material/process substitution, enclosure/local exhaust/HEPA filtration, maintenance and operating procedures. NIOSH reports large particle-emission reductions from effective filtered enclosures and local exhaust in cited studies; that does not mean any generic consumer enclosure has the same performance:
- https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/docs/2024-103/
- https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/bulletin/2024/safe-3d-printing.html

UL 2904 Edition 2 is an active method for assessing particle and chemical emissions from printers intended for non-industrial indoor environments, including residential settings:
https://www.shopulstandards.com/ProductDetail.aspx?productId=UL2904_2_S_20230526

Therefore:
- no assumption that PLA or a low-odour filament is automatically safe for unrestricted indoor printing;
- a household node must use a documented printer/material/operating envelope, source-controlled enclosure and ventilation arrangement, and an appropriate safety review;
- no resin/vat-photopolymerization equipment in the initial household pilot (uncured resin, solvents, post-cure and waste need a separate chemical-control work package);
- no printer in bedrooms or other occupied living spaces for the initial pilot; prefer a qualified community hub where adequate source-control ventilation cannot be assured;
- no PVC or unknown feedstocks; do not infer low emissions from marketing claims;
- emissions testing and health/safety compliance are separate from part mechanical qualification.

### South African capability already exists

The CSIR's Advanced Design and Manufacturing Innovation Centre (ADMIC) supports SMMEs with additive manufacturing, polymer/powder processes, 3D scanning, design and product-lifecycle workflows. The CSIR's Collaborative Programme in Additive Manufacturing (CPAM) supports AM research, capability development and industrialisation. Its calls and funding windows are time-limited; no current funding eligibility or partner access is assumed:
- https://www.csir.co.za/advanced-design-and-manufacturing-innovation-centre
- https://www.csir.co.za/call-proposals-collaborative-programme-additive-manufacturing
- https://www.csir.co.za/what-we-do/manufacturing

This means we should build a network that connects households and SMMEs to existing facilities rather than duplicate capital-intensive infrastructure.

## Paradigm shift: from printer ownership to qualified local production capability

Do not measure success by the number of home printers sold. Measure how many useful repairs can be completed safely, affordably and repeatably.

Use a tiered capability model; it is a local programme profile informed by ISO/ASTM 52966:2026, not a claim to be certified under that standard:

### H0 — household participation
- Browse and request rights-cleared part designs.
- Print only approved low-consequence cosmetic/organisational accessories where the printer/material/room setup and user training meet the published H0 envelope.
- Perform simple, documented assembly/maintenance tasks and verify identity.
- No household acceptance or installation of safety-critical, pressure-bearing, high-temperature, mains-electrical, flame-protective, food/water-contact or high-load components.

### N1 — neighbourhood fabrication hub
- Enclosed FDM/material-extrusion machines with measured process profile and source-controlled ventilation.
- Trained operator; managed materials/lot storage and printer calibration.
- Dimensional inspection, weighing, post-processing and documented acceptance.
- Produce approved low-risk functional spares only when the part profile explicitly permits N1 and the hub meets the process/material/inspection requirements.
- Provide scanning and repair assistance without assuming a scan automatically grants design rights or technical equivalence.

### R2 — regional qualified manufacturing partner
- More capable polymer AM, CNC, laser/sheet fabrication, forming, moulding and specialist metrology.
- Controlled materials, equipment, operators, inspection and process capability.
- Parts requiring tighter tolerances, environmental resistance, load or functional testing must be routed here or to a suitable OEM/contract manufacturer.

### Q3 — original-equipment / qualified industrial production
- Motors, impellers, blades, guards, mains enclosures and insulation systems, pressure vessels, hot-water components, refrigerant components, structural/load-bearing parts, safety-critical electronics and other high-consequence components.
- Use qualified suppliers, controlled industrial processes and product-specific evidence/conformity routes.
- A file in the catalogue never authorizes household or neighbourhood manufacture of a P3 part.

A part is assigned to the minimum tier that can satisfy the complete use-case and acceptance requirements—not the tier with the cheapest machine.

## Part admission and safety classification

Build a part admission process using consequence of failure, operating environment, material/process uncertainty, rights, inspection capability and post-repair verification.

Initial part classes:
- **P0 — non-functional / cosmetic / organisational:** storage dividers, cosmetic trim, labels, non-load-bearing organisers and workshop aids. These are the initial home-print candidates, subject to IP and emissions controls.
- **P1 — low-consequence functional:** selected non-safety clips, covers or service accessories with bounded loads/environment. Only admitted after documented material/process envelope, tolerance and failure review. H0 access is opt-in and limited to the exact released file and conditions.
- **P2 — engineered functional / service-critical:** parts whose failure may damage the appliance, compromise a function, or introduce elevated thermal, mechanical, chemical or electrical hazards. Neighbourhood/regional production only after part-specific verification and authorized post-repair checks; no generic blanket approval.
- **P3 — safety-critical / regulated / high-consequence:** no H0 or unqualified N1 production. Includes mains insulation/enclosures, guards around moving parts, blades/rotors/impellers, pressure or hot-water containment, refrigerant circuit parts, hot surfaces, structural loads, fire barriers, medical/water-quality/food-contact surfaces and any part whose failure can cause shock, fire, scald, entrapment, contamination or serious injury. Use the OEM or competent qualified industrial route and applicable conformity review.

This classification is a proposed risk-screening structure, not a substitute for a formal product hazard analysis or regulatory decision. The exact appliance manufacturer / designer retains responsibility for the part's function and compatibility; Luminous cannot convert a P3 component into a home-printable part by changing a label.

## Part digital package — design-to-accepted-repair

For each admitted part, define a rights-cleared, machine-readable package containing:
- stable part ID, exact appliance model/SKU/revision compatibility and supersession/effectivity;
- permitted part class and production tiers (H0/N1/R2/Q3);
- functional requirements, prohibited uses, failure consequences and operating envelope;
- source CAD / neutral geometry, drawing, critical dimensions, tolerances and inspection datum;
- design licence / manufacturing rights, authorship, source provenance and redistribution conditions;
- material specification, supplier and lot identity, drying/conditioning requirements, storage and expiry where relevant;
- printer/process capability profile, nozzle/hot-end, build volume, calibration, firmware, slicer version/profile, orientation, supports, layer parameters and permitted process window;
- approved build file digest; do not treat an arbitrary user-edited G-code file as an approved equivalent;
- build environment and safety-control requirements;
- coupons or witness specimens and the exact mechanical/thermal/environmental tests required for the part class;
- dimensional/visual inspection and acceptance criteria;
- post-processing and forbidden operations;
- printed-part ID and production receipt binding design/material/printer/operator/process/inspection;
- installation instructions, required qualification/skill, repair preconditions and post-repair functional checks;
- source/test evidence, uncertainty, limitations, date, review/expiry and change-trigger rules.

Use Mycelix's existing provenance and manufacturing records for receipts and identities; use Symthaea's MFG-PROC-000 for process/capability semantics; do not create another product passport, MES or inventory ledger.

A file hash proves the identity of bytes, not engineering correctness, intellectual-property permission, material quality or a part's suitability.

## First product pilot: low-risk parts and manufacturing aids

Use the fan microfactory as the first vertical, but explicitly avoid printing fan safety parts.

Initial candidate set:
- assembly alignment and drilling jigs;
- non-electrical cable/connector placement aids used only during controlled assembly;
- inspection go/no-go gauges where their reference surfaces and tolerances are verified;
- packaging dunnage and transport spacers;
- non-functional cosmetic caps and trim;
- selected non-load-bearing service/organisation accessories.

Only after the qualification workflow works should we evaluate a small set of P1 replacement parts such as a specific clip or cover with bounded environmental exposure and no guard/electrical/thermal function. The designer must approve each exact part ID and process/material profile. Do not start with fan guards, blades, impellers, motor mounts, mains enclosures, hot-water fittings, dishwasher wetted parts or washing-machine load-bearing parts.

## Benchmark: local fabrication versus OEM / conventional supply

For each exact part and repair task compare:
1. OEM spare part / official service route;
2. conventional local fabrication (CNC, sheet metal, moulding or workshop route);
3. neighbourhood additive route;
4. household additive route where H0 admits it.

Freeze the same part function, fit, interface, operating exposure and post-repair check. Report:
- time from repair request to conforming part available;
- total restoration time and service downtime;
- full cost per accepted part: material, failed prints, machine depreciation, electricity, operator time, inspection, finishing, transport, repair and warranty/rework reserve;
- dimensional accuracy and critical feature uncertainty;
- mechanical performance in declared orientations / build axes;
- thermal, moisture, UV, chemical, fatigue/creep and vibration behaviour where relevant;
- first-pass yield, reprint rate, rejection, rework and recurrence;
- energy, material consumed, scrap / support waste and actual recycled-content evidence;
- local sourcing, parts fill rate, lead-time distribution and supply disruption recovery;
- rights/compatibility/security completeness and traceability;
- success of post-repair functional requalification.

Do not assume additive wins on cost or environmental impact. For high-volume parts, injection moulding or conventional manufacturing may be materially cheaper and more consistent. The likely additive advantage is low-volume, diverse, customised or obsolete spares where tooling and inventory are expensive.

## Proposed benchmark targets — hypotheses, not results

- 100% of catalogued files have documented manufacturing rights, exact compatibility and part class before distribution.
- 100% of prints have traceable design/material/printer/process/inspection identity at the tier required by the part.
- Zero P3-risk part designs admitted to H0 and zero safety-critical parts installed without the designated competent qualification route.
- 100% rejection of seeded wrong-revision, wrong-material, expired/unknown material, incompatible printer/process, altered-build-file, missing-calibration and failed-inspection cases.
- At least three independent printer/operator nodes reproduce a selected low-risk part with declared dimensional and functional acceptance; sample counts for confirmatory reliability claims are determined after pilot variance.
- Target at least 25% lower median and P90 time-to-part-restoration for a selected low-volume / obsolete part set versus the observed local OEM route, without safety, fit/function, recurrence or lifecycle-cost regressions. This is a stretch hypothesis to test after the baseline is measured.
- Publish cost per accepted part at 1, 3, 10, 50 and 100 annual parts, retaining failed attempts, inspection and all non-print costs.
- Report environmental and material balances rather than assuming that printed parts or recycled filament are sustainable.

## Execution sequence

1. Reuse #6603's Stage 1 FDM printer provision for fixtures; publish the H0/N1/R2/P3 part admission and safety boundary before any household-part catalogue.
2. Use #5686 to register material-extrusion capability profiles, process recipes, preconditions, result and qualification semantics. Keep machine execution authority in its existing owner.
3. Build one part digital package and one fixture/part acceptance workflow for the fan programme.
4. Discover existing South African facilities (starting with CSIR ADMIC/CPAM and nearby SMME printing bureaus) and verify their actual processes, materials, metrology, service availability, rights/data terms, cost and lead time. The CSIR pages are discovery leads, not confirmed partners.
5. Compare household printer ownership versus neighbourhood access versus regional partner access using measured demand, utilization, full lifetime costs, access distance and failure/maintenance burden.
6. Only then decide whether one household demonstration printer is appropriate. Do not buy machines or launch a user-facing manufacturing service from desk price estimates alone.
7. Expand to household accessories and selected low-risk repair parts; keep appliances' P2/P3 parts under qualified engineering control.

## Claim ceiling

This issue is a research and qualification plan. It does not establish a printer deployment, safe domestic emissions profile, qualified material/process, licensed part catalogue, repair-rights permission, partner relationship, print accuracy, part performance, reduced lifecycle cost, production yield or product conformity. No household or community network exists merely because the architecture is described.
